statement: The first half of this session gives a brief overview of non-relational databases: where to use each type and, more importantly, where not to use it.
detail: The teacher puts more weight on where a database should NOT be used.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So first half, I'll give a brief overview of non-relational databases and not just that, okay, this is where you have to use it.

statement: The advice to always use NoSQL databases is not true; many people promote their non-relational databases as challenging the relational database, but most databases out there are meant to solve very specific problems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you'll find a ton of databases out there meant to solve very specific problems.

statement: Today only scratches the surface of non-relational databases; they lay the foundation for later topics, and the course goes deeper into each type in later weeks (fifth, sixth week), with granular nitty-gritty details along the way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we are just scratching the surface today with respect to non-relational databases, because they lay the foundation for us to build other stuff

statement: The first half runs roughly 1 hour 5 to 1 hour 10 minutes; the second half is a long discussion designing Slack's real-time communication, limited to text-based communication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And then a huge discussion on Slack's real-time communication. And we'll only do text-based communication.

statement: In the same Slack real-time communication design one can easily switch from one message delivery model to another, so the same design yields WhatsApp, Slack or Zoom chat (and Instagram); once Slack is done these become a piece of cake.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in this same design, you would see how we can design something like a WhatsApp, something like Slack, something like Zoom chat.

statement: System design is about recognising patterns, the Lego blocks, and assembling them into a running system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: system design is just about looking at those patterns, looking at those Lego blocks.

statement: Computer science mirrors how humans operate: working on patterns, learning from them and iterating; the von Neumann architecture of the first CPUs has many similarities to how the brain functions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you see the von Neumann architecture of the first CPU set, it's exactly how our brain functions.

statement: There should not really be a term like 'non-relational' or 'NoSQL' database; always name the specific type of database instead of blanketing everything that is not MySQL, Postgres or Oracle.
detail: The teacher compares it to labelling people 'technical' and 'non-technical', which is offensive to non-technical folks.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we should always refer to the specific type of database that we are talking about

statement: 'NoSQL databases scale' is wrong as a blanket statement: one can build a non-relational database that does not scale at all, and the teacher promises examples of such databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I can build a non-relational database which does not scale at all. Very much possible.

statement: It is important to understand the different types of databases beyond the famous MySQL and Postgres, so you know where a particular type should be used.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's very important to understand different types of databases that are out there, apart from the famous MySQL and Postgres of the world.

statement: The teacher uses the terms 'NoSQL' / 'non-relational' only in this general introduction, because that is how people talk; afterwards he always names the exact type of database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'll be just using this term in this one. After that, I'll never use it, because I don't like to just blanket it out.

statement: The very general distinction is that non-relational (NoSQL) databases are not relationally structured, though nothing stops someone from structuring them relationally, which is why the space is messy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a very general distinction between relational and non-relational, or SQL and non-SQL, or NoSQL databases, is that they are not relationally structured.

statement: As a very broad, not-always-true separation, non-relational databases typically give up consistency to give you scalability.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a very broad separation is that non-relational databases typically give up consistency to give you scalability.

statement: There are two kinds of consistency: consistency in the CAP theorem is different from consistency in ACID (computer scientists are bad at naming things).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The consistency in CAP theorem is different from consistency in ACID.

statement: Consistency in ACID is about the data being correct: you do not mess with it and the database moves from one correct state to another.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Consistency in ACID is about data being consistent, strongly consistent, where you don't mess with that and you move from one correct state to another.

statement: Consistency in the CAP theorem is about data being visible / available to query right away (strong consistency); this is the consistency non-relational databases give up.
detail: 'So here the consistency that we are talking about is this other one' - the CAP one.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: that consistency is about your data being shown, being available to query right there in it

statement: Non-relational databases typically let you scale horizontally and be highly available, because there are multiple nodes, by compromising on consistency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: horizontally scale the system and be highly available, because there are multiple nodes now, by compromising on consistency.

statement: Relational databases wanted all the data in one database instance, so if that instance goes down the whole system is down and is not highly available.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Relational databases wanted all the data to be there in one shot, in one database instance. So if that goes down, the system is down.

statement: Non-relational databases spread data out horizontally, so if one node goes down other nodes still serve the data and there is almost never a complete downtime.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Even if one of the node goes down, you have other nodes to serve the data.

statement: Non-relational databases give up strong consistency and become eventually consistent; most are eventually consistent, but there are always exceptions because there is no standardization.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So most non-relational databases are eventual, but you would always find exceptions, because there is no standardization.

statement: Cassandra, MongoDB and DynamoDB do scale, but each only for a very specific workload.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I agree Cassandra scales, but for a very specific workload, MongoDB scales for a very specific workload, DynamoDB scales for a very specific workload.

statement: It is a very big misconception that relational databases don't scale; you just need to know how to use them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a very big misconception where people say relational databases don't scale. You just need to know how to use it.

statement: The previous session's distributed key-value store sharded relational databases (one holding keys A to M, another N to Z), giving up consistency to get an almost highly available, horizontally scalable system - exactly what non-relational databases do.
case_study: The distributed key-value store built in the previous session.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We split our databases where one database hold keys from A to M, second did hold keys from N to Z, right?

statement: Give up the constraints that do not help you scale horizontally and you have a truly horizontally scalable relational database; saying only non-relational databases scale is crude.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You give up on constraints that is not helping you scale horizontally, and you have a truly horizontally scalable relational database.

statement: Never believe a generic statement at face value, even from the teacher: demand that it be specific and contextual, ask critical questions, and remember a counter-example can always be found; this makes you a better engineer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: anytime when you hear a generic statement, even from me, from anyone, don't believe it. Never.

statement: Document databases are the type of non-relational database closest to the relational world; famous examples are MongoDB and Elasticsearch.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They are called document databases. Now document databases, very famous examples, MongoDB, Elasticsearch.

statement: Storing a value as JSON and wanting to query within it (as discussed in the previous session) is exactly what document databases give you.
case_study: Ties to the previous session's key-value store with JSON values.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm storing my value as a JSON and I want to query within that. That's exactly what document databases give you.

statement: Document databases are mostly JSON based, though there is no hard and fast rule.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They are mostly JSON based. There is no hard and fast rule, but they are mostly JSON based.

statement: Document databases support complex queries, e.g. aggregations on MongoDB and faceted queries on Elasticsearch.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They support complex queries. On MongoDB, you can do aggregations on Elasticsearch, you can do faceted query on Elasticsearch.

statement: Document databases are not exactly as powerful as relational ones but close, so when people move a generic relational schema to the non-relational world they typically adopt a document database, almost never jumping directly to a key-value store.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You would never see them drastically moving from this to a direct key-value store, right?

statement: A key-value store is very restrictive because you do not peek into the value, so it is of no use unless the use case fits exactly that access pattern.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because it's very restrictive, where you do not peek into the value, then it's of no use unless the use case was exactly like that.

statement: A key feature of document databases is querying on document attributes, e.g. 'give me all documents with this attribute set to this value' in MongoDB or Elasticsearch.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: give me all the documents having this particular attribute set to this particular value.

statement: Document databases allow partial updates: you can update just one attribute of a document.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can make partial updates to the document. You can say that, hey, in this document, just update this one attribute.

statement: In a key-value store the value is just a blob, so updating it means read, update and write; partial updates are not possible, while document databases typically allow them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: where value is just a blob, you, if you'd want to do an update, you have to read, update and write.

statement: DynamoDB is a key-value store, not a document database, yet it still allows you to query within the document.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you would know that DynamoDB is a key-value store. It's not a document based database, but still allows you to query within the document, right?

statement: There is no line separating document databases, key-value stores and columnar storage; lines are very blurry because every database is entering every other database's space.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is no line that separates document DBs and key-value stores and columnar storages and whatnot. It's very blurry.

statement: Understand the access pattern and the features (e.g. complex queries, partial updates) rather than the label of a database type.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So which is why understand the access pattern, understand the features

statement: As an engineer, know which features you want from a database and which database gives you that; generic claims about databases never work because something true today can be completely false later.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what you need to know as an engineer is what features do you want from the database and which database gives you that.

statement: MongoDB started out saying 'we are BASE, not ACID', but is now ACID compliant, though maybe not as optimally as the SQL world.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They started to say, hey, we are BASE. We are not ACID, right? But now MongoDB is ACID compliant.

statement: Key-value stores are more restrictive than document databases: every operation is key-wise, e.g. get a key, put a key, delete a key, insert a key, insert a value into the set represented by a key.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they are always key wise operations, like get a key, put a key, delete a key, insert a key

statement: Because every operation is key-wise, a key-value store can be sharded very easily: you never have to make cross-shard queries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But because everything is key wise, you can very easily shard the database, because you would never have to make cross shard queries.

statement: Cross-shard queries arise with range operations or the IN operator: 'documents where ID in 1, 2, 3' may hit three different databases, which is very expensive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: give me all the documents where ID in 1, 2 and 3. What if one is on one database, two is on this database

statement: Because a key-value store limits access to single-key operations, it can be very heavily partitioned - thousands and thousands of partitions - without any hiccups.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: key-value store you can very heavily partition, very heavily, like thousands and thousands of partitions without having any hiccups

statement: The more complex you make the queries, the less you can distribute the data, because cross-shard queries become expensive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the more complex you make these queries, the lesser you can distribute the data, because then cross-shard queries become expensive.

statement: Document databases typically do support cross-partition operations, but they become really expensive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: database typically support that, but it becomes really expensive for you to do that

statement: By limiting access, key-value stores get massive parallelism: with many databases, each handles queries in parallel without waiting for others, giving the best performance at the cost of restricted access.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: by limiting the access, you get massive parallelism.

statement: Every single thing in computer science is a trade-off: you get something, you lose something.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: How every single thing is a trade-off. You get something, you lose something.

statement: Key-value stores lose the power of complex queries but gain massive parallelization and availability; document databases keep complex features but cannot have thousands and thousands of partitions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Here with key-value store, you lost the power of making complex queries, but you gained massive parallelization, massive availability and whatnot.

statement: Column-oriented databases (a type the teacher is personally a fan of) exploit how people query the system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Column oriented databases, they exploit how people queries the system.

statement: In row-oriented databases all the columns (attributes) of a row sit together; that is also how we usually draw a table.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: all the columns of that particular row, all the attributes of the particular row, they sit together. Those are row oriented databases.

statement: Running example: a 'stock ticks' table with the prices of all listed stocks, columns symbol, price, name, exchange and timestamp, one entry per tick.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a table called stock ticks where I'm putting the stock prices of all the stocks listed. I have symbol, price, name, exchange and timestamp.

statement: In a row-oriented database the five columns of a row are stacked one after another and persisted as one row on disk, so even when you select only two columns the disk reads the entire row, then the engine filters what you need.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: on the disk side, it is actually reading the entire row because this entire thing is stacked together.

statement: Column-oriented databases stack the values of one column across multiple rows together (the three values of column 1 sit together, then those of column 2, ...).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they stack the columns across multiple rows together.

statement: A crude, naive mental model of a column store: one separate file per column, where line n holds that column's value for row n.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: assume that you have one file for each column, one separate file for each column. It's a very naive way

statement: Query on the stock ticks table: the average price of the entire stock market for a particular day, i.e. SELECT AVG(price) WHERE timestamp = something.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Select average of price where timestamp equal to something.

statement: In a row-oriented store, with say 10,000 listed companies there are about 10,000 entries for the date; the engine goes through each row, reads it, picks timestamp and price, and averages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's say I have 10,000 companies listed for a particular date, I might have 10,000 entries

statement: For that query a row store unnecessarily reads symbol, name and exchange, wasting disk IO: even if they are not projected in the SELECT, the engine still has to skim through them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because you are not projecting it from the select, but your database engine has to still go through that

statement: A row store must pass over unneeded columns because unless it knows the row boundary it cannot pick the corresponding columns.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: unless it knows this is my row boundary, it cannot pick the corresponding columns.

statement: Data warehouses have thousands of columns (the teacher stresses he is not exaggerating).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Data warehouses have thousands of columns.

statement: If your use case is very likely to query only a few of many columns - the classic analytics query - column-oriented databases work well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are very likely or extremely likely to just query on few of the columns, column oriented databases work well.

statement: On a column store the average-price query reads only two files, price and timestamp; no disk IO at all is done for symbol, name and exchange, which is extremely efficient.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So literally the only two files that I would be reading, price and timestamp.

statement: Because they thrive when operating on few of hundreds or thousands of columns, column-oriented databases power data warehouses such as Amazon Redshift and Google BigQuery.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which is where you would always find them being used for data warehouses, Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, all of them.

statement: In data engineering, file formats such as Parquet leverage column-oriented storage so you read the bare minimum.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You may have heard of Parquet. All of them leverage column oriented storages

statement: You can, but should not, build a transactional application such as a blogging app on a column-oriented database, because you almost always read the entire row (e.g. rendering a user profile is a SELECT * over its 10-15 columns).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you should not build blogging application on column oriented databases. Why? Because you are very likely to read the entire row.

statement: Transactional use cases fit row-oriented storage; analytics use cases fit column-oriented storage because they pick very few columns, two, three or 10 out of a thousand.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: analytics use case fit more over here, because you are very picky in picking columns, two out of thousand or three out of thousand

statement: Go find which data warehouse your company uses (every company has one, most likely BigQuery or Redshift - people don't typically build them), or ask a data engineer friend about the Parquet format and see how it optimizes storage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every company has a data warehouse, every single, right? Go find which data warehouse your company is.

statement: Just by altering the way data is stored you get a massive performance boost without changing the layers above - the beauty of having abstractions in the right place.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: just by altering the way storage, like altering the way you're storing the data, you get massive performance boost without even changing the above layers.

statement: Strongly recommended reading: the paper 'C-Store: A Column-oriented DBMS' - the sixth paper the teacher ever read, in his master's databases course - to see how column-oriented databases were conceptualized; a breezy read that can be finished in about four days, brilliantly written.
detail: It shows how deep researchers go into a problem; big things are conveyed in one line. It made the teacher fall in love with research. Other papers he read and annotated are on his website.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: C-store, a column-oriented DBMS. Just Google.

statement: Do not build a habit of getting spoon-fed: search for things like the paper yourself.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just Google.

statement: Asked whether a SELECT that names specific columns still reads all columns: in a row-oriented database the disk still reads all columns and the engine picks out the ones you need; a column-oriented database does not read the columns you don't need (think separate files).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: From the disk, it reads all the columns, picks out the ones that you need.

statement: A student pointed out that insertion would be too heavy in column-oriented databases; the teacher agreed - you get some, you lose some - and said it is okay given the benefits.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: One minor drawback that I see for column-oriented databases is that insertion would be too heavy.

statement: Column-oriented databases are never used as the primary database; they serve analytics workloads, and the data warehouse is never the primary copy of the data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So data warehouse is never your primary copy of the data.

statement: The primary copy lives in traditional databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB); a job ingests the data from there into the column-oriented data warehouse just to power analytics.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: From there you move data into a column-oriented database. Right. Just to power the raw analytics.

statement: Asked about space: column-oriented data can be compressed very heavily because each column is homogeneous (e.g. timestamps are almost discrete values), so it needs much less space; row-oriented data is heterogeneous, so compression helps less.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can so heavily compress this because it's a homogeneous data, right?

statement: A 29x compression gain is normal for column-oriented storage in the teacher's experience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And if I tell you a factor, 29x is a normal gain that I'm seeing.

statement: Stock symbols (Apple, Google, ...) are a small set of discrete values, so instead of storing the full string each value can be represented by a small fixed-size code (the teacher says one byte, then four bytes), giving heavy compression.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can get very heavy compression because it is homogeneous data, because there is not much variation in that.
flags: check: garbled passage "APP, LG, 00", "one byte ... four byte"

statement: Huffman, Snappy and LZ compression work really well on column data because it is very homogeneous (not a mix of strings and integers).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So Huffman compression works well. Snappy compression works really well. LZ compression works really well.

statement: The database engine handles compression itself: you pass normal strings and it compresses internally, e.g. a column with five or six distinct values can be represented in one byte.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can just pass in the normal string that you are passing, but internally, it can very heavily compress the data.

statement: Read about run-length encoding.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Read about run length encoding once.

statement: Asked whether column-oriented databases are charged per read/write operation like cloud NoSQL databases: no - they run continuously, you pre-provision capacity and pay for the servers you run; IOPS are charged but it is not per-operation on-demand pricing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, column-oriented databases continuously run. So you have to pre-provision the capacity that you need.

statement: A student summarised column-oriented database pricing as reserved capacity; the teacher agreed it was put better that way.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: It's a reserved capacity. Yeah, there you may put it better.

statement: Graph databases are one of the most misunderstood databases: for a Twitter-like follow/following relationship people reach for a graph database because it can be visualized as a graph, but it might not be the best choice.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because you can visualize it as a graph, which is where you think, hey, graph databases. But they might not be the best choice.

statement: A graph database is literally the graph data structure from the college DSA course: the adjacency-list representation stored as is, with data APIs exposed on top - nothing special.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just move that exact same adjacency list representation in so and expose data APIs out of it, and that became graph database.

statement: Graph databases specialise in (sophisticated) graph algorithms.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: these databases, they are specialized in graph algorithms.

statement: LinkedIn showing how far a person is from you (first, second, third, fourth connection) is a sophisticated graph algorithm; modelling social behaviour and recommendations are others.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That is a sophisticated graph algorithm.

statement: Using a graph database whenever a use case can be visualised as a graph is the worst way to think; modelling follow/following on a graph database could be catastrophic - strong word, but really expensive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Modeling a follow following relationship on a graph database could be catastrophic.

statement: Scaling graph databases is very difficult: they are extremely memory intensive, most are built on a legacy stack, and even modern-language ones are not very optimal.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Scaling graph databases, very difficult. Difficult, they are extremely memory intensive

statement: This does not mean you should not use graph databases: whenever you need core graph algorithms, go for a graph database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever you need core graph algorithms, go for graph databases.

statement: Using a graph database just to store follow/following data is like using the Hulk to open a glass jar: it gives you much more than this tiny, trivial use case needs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's like using Hulk to open a glass or to open a jar, a glass jar, right?

statement: Recommendations - basic collaborative filtering - are where graph databases thrive and are the most common use.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Like basic collaborative filtering is one of the application where you see graph databases thrive.

statement: The teacher has a detailed YouTube video on recommendations with graph databases, but covers more in class than in the video.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I have a video on it, a detailed video on it, you may find it on my YouTube anyway

statement: Collaborative filtering, a popular approach to driving recommendations: if you and I are similar users and you purchased something on Amazon, Amazon should recommend it to me.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's say you purchased something on Amazon and you and I are similar users. Amazon should recommend what you purchased to me.

statement: E-commerce first builds cohorts of similar users via the graph: with a product node such as iPhone, everyone who bought an iPhone forms a similar set; if one of them buys AirPods, Amazon can recommend AirPods to everyone else in the cohort.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now if one of them purchases AirPods, Amazon can recommend AirPods to everyone else in the cohort.

statement: The one-level example is simplified: real cohort building happens two or three levels deep, which is hard to model outside a graph.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm just giving example of one level. It happens at two or three level deep.

statement: Most machine learning teams and organisations do exactly this; recommendations are a classic case driven through graph databases because they need these capabilities.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Most machine learning teams and organizations do this exact same thing.

statement: Fraud detection is the best, far more important and interesting use case for graph databases; it shows their true power.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: fraud detection, best use case for graph databases.

statement: About a year and a half ago the teacher bought a Grammarly subscription with his credit card; right after triggering the OTP he got a call from HDFC Bank asking whether he was making the transaction, confirmed it, and the payment went through - and wondered how they retrieved this so quickly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I immediately got a call from HDFC Bank. They said, hey, are you trying to make this transaction?

statement: Graph-based fraud detection: someone whose transactions have all been domestic suddenly makes an international one; it is an odd one out, a new edge outside their closely knit cluster/network, which a graph database flags very quickly as suspicious.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's a new edge that is being created that is suspicious.

statement: Financial companies categorise every transaction along 50-60 parameters (country, region, type of products purchased, things interacted with, ...), ingest them into a graph so almost every person has an independent graph, and when a new edge appears outside it they compute a degree of suspicion and predict whether the transaction is suspicious.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every person almost has its own independent graph ready.

statement: The whole fraud check must be done within a 200 millisecond SLA.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And all of this is, has to be done in 200 milliseconds. That's it. They have 200 millisecond SLA.

statement: The source of the 200 ms figure: an actual VP of engineering at JP Morgan Chase, a participant in the fifth cohort, explained this use case; the details are sensitive and cannot be shared.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: actual VP engineering of JP Morgan Chase, took this cohort, fifth cohort, and he explained this use case.

statement: Within the 200 ms the bank decides and redirects the case to a customer executive, who calls you to confirm you are making the transaction; once approved you can proceed. The whole system is powered by graph analysis.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in 200 milliseconds, they have to make this decision and they have to redirect it to the customer executive.

statement: If you can visualise something as a graph, more often than not that is NOT where you should use a graph database (follow/following is trivial); use one where you need actual raw graph algorithms.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: most more often than not, that is not where you should be using graph databases.

statement: Neo4j is one of the first graph databases to come out (one of the first, not the best).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Few examples, Neo4j, one of the best, like one of the first, not the best, one of the first that came out.

statement: AWS, which 'copies everything', has its own managed graph database offering called Neptune.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: AWS has their own managed offering from graph database called Neptune.

statement: Dgraph is written in Go and works well at moderate scale but falters a bit at high scale; the teacher used it very extensively and it was one of the first projects he read to understand Go.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: High scale it falters a bit. I use Dgraph very extensively.

statement: The Dgraph team also has an embedded database called BadgerDB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And they have an embedded database called BadgerDB. Also fascinating.

statement: TigerGraph is a proprietary graph database used by a lot of financial companies, which do not rely on open-source software for this.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A lot of companies, a lot of financial companies actually use TigerGraph.

statement: These were the basics of non-relational databases as an introduction; each of them will be used in the coming weeks.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And we will use each one of them in the coming weeks.

statement: Non-relational databases scale because there are no relations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why non-relational databases scale? They scale because there are no relations.

statement: Foreign key constraints ensure correctness: with a non-null foreign key you cannot insert a row whose referenced row does not exist.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are not allowed to insert the row where that other row is not present.

statement: Similarly for deletion: parent entries cannot be deleted until all child entries are deleted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: unless you delete all the child entries, parent entries cannot be deleted.

statement: Relational databases ensure correctness and strong consistency - moving from one consistent state to another - by enforcing relations and constraints on the data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they try to ensure the correctness of the system, the strong consistency of the data

statement: Non-relational databases give up on enforcing relations: they don't care what you insert or whether a referenced key exists.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I don't care what you insert. I don't care if that key exists or not. Just insert the data that you want.

statement: Relational databases chose correctness because their first use cases were financial, where correctness of data mattered more than performing at scale; this does not make them worse than non-relational databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: first set of use case that they were built on was financial use case where correctness of the data was more important

statement: Every database has a backstory explaining its design decisions, and you should be aware of it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Everyone has a backstory. This is the backstory of relational databases and why they made a certain decision.

statement: Relational databases chose data consistency and strong consistency over a high ingestion rate.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: data consistency and strong consistency over high ingestion rate

statement: To scale a relational database, just don't use foreign keys / constraints; then you can partition it exactly like a non-relational database, which never gives you those features anyway.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if you'd want to scale this, just don't use foreign key. Simple.

statement: When a database claims to be great at something, understand why and what it gives up to get there, and see if you can mimic the same on the database you know, SQL or not.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: understand why they are being great at certain things, what kind of things that they give up in order to get that.

statement: Never be stuck with a particular technology ('I only use this, every other database sucks'): every database is unique in its own flavour; look beneath the fancy UI to see why it performs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So never just be stuck with a particular technology.

statement: SQL's strength is data correctness / strong consistency: when correctness of data is the most important feature of your application you need ACID, and if you need ACID go for SQL.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The strength of SQL data correctness slash consistency, strong consistency, right?
flags: unclear: "when do you see a comment"

statement: SQL databases give you the tooling (foreign key checks, check constraints, ...) to keep data from ever reaching an inconsistent or incorrect state, but it is not automatic: you have to apply them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So having those foreign key checks, check constraints and whatnot, you have to apply them

statement: Use NoSQL when you have gigantic data to ingest at a fast pace, e.g. a huge influx of messages on Instagram, posts being written, logs being dumped, metrics.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A very simple way to look at it is when you have gigantic data, gigantic data.

statement: Such ingestion use cases do not optimise for correctness: it is okay if a datum is here or there, an attribute is missing or some data is lost (metrics, logs, message ingestion).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's okay. If one of the data is here or there, one attribute is missing.

statement: Cassandra suits high-speed ingestion because it gives sharding out of the box and drops constraints, so it is light on the database and heavily partitioned.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: for example Cassandra, because it gives you sharding and whatnot out of the box and it drops those constraints.

statement: Messaging systems, live interactions, pollings and the like typically store data in non-relational databases because sharding/partitioning come out of the box and constraints are dropped; with SQL you would have to build those yourself.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you are using SQL, you would have to build them on your own.

statement: Broad summary: when correctness and consistency matter and you want that tooling out of the box, go for SQL; for a high ingestion rate and sharding out of the box, go for a NoSQL database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you need sharding, you need very high ingestion and whatnot. You go for NoSQL database.

statement: Throughout the course every database choice weighs all these factors; don't be rigid on a particular database or say 'I will use NoSQL everywhere'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: don't be rigid on a particular database.

statement: Asked how a graph database stores adjacency lists with a varying number of neighbours: via its storage engine, serialized on disk (not in memory); it depends on the database, but think of it bluntly as a comma-separated list of IDs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: think of it as a comma separated list of IDs, a blunt implementation.

statement: A student suggested a graph database is then basically a KV store; the teacher agreed and added that every database can be modelled on top of a KV store.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Right. So it's a KV store basically.

statement: The KV store is the NAND gate of databases: just as AND, OR, NOT and all gates can be built from NAND, every database can be modelled on top of a KV store, though maybe not as performantly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: KV store is a NAND gate of the databases, like how you can implement and, or, not, not, all the gates with NAND gate.

statement: A graph database cannot be used transactionally by user-facing applications: you ingest data into it asynchronously and then derive something from it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So actually transactionally, you cannot use it. You ingest it asynchronously and then drive something out of it.

statement: A student added that applications typically create those models on top of relational or non-relational databases; the teacher said 'Correct'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Typically create those models on top of relational or non-relational databases.
flags: check: meaning of student's statement unclear

statement: Why a graph database instead of relational: finding something three levels deep is a simple graph traversal query, while in a relational database N levels deep needs N self-joins, and the query must be rewritten for each depth - painful.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In relational databases for N level deep, you have to write N self...

statement: N self-joins on a table may not be very optimal when the data is huge.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Plus n self joins on a table may not be very optimal when your data is huge.

statement: A relational database stores data on one data node; sharding exists, but graph databases give it to you out of the box.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Third, your data is stored in one data node in terms of relational DB.

statement: For real-world references, search 'fraud detection graph databases' or 'graph databases in recommendation engine'; there are tons of articles.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: fraud detection, graph databases in recommendation engine, you'll find tons of articles above.

statement: Asked about MongoDB now offering ACID: MongoDB's official documentation says to use ACID sparingly, because cross-shard ACID is implemented with distributed transactions, which slow down throughput.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In their official documentation, it says that please use ACID sparingly.
flags: check: possibly the Teacher answering ("not performant"?) - diarization

statement: ACID within a single shard anyone can guarantee; cross-shard ACID is only done through distributed transactions, which slow down throughput, so avoid it when you need high throughput.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Within shard ACID, anyone can guarantee.

statement: The same advice appears in WiredTiger's documentation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And I've also found it in the WiredTiger's documentation as well.

statement: Asked whether 'no relations' is what decides putting a KV store on SQL vs non-SQL: no - KV stores are databases in their own league; KV is just an access pattern that does not define the underlying store.
case_study: Ties to the previous session's KV store built on a relational database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: KV is just an access pattern. It does not define the underlying store.

statement: DynamoDB and Redis are both key-value stores with different storage engines: Redis keeps data in memory, DynamoDB on disk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis does it in memory. DynamoDB does it on disk.

statement: For a KV access-pattern use case, besides correctness, you can go for a specialised KV store such as DynamoDB or Redis; understand the features you need, since you may not need to build a KV store from scratch.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because you may not always need to build a KV store from scratch, because KV is just an access pattern.
flags: check: "Correct." inside the student's turn at 00:52:14

statement: Whether a KV store on a relational database, DynamoDB or Redis scale the same depends on what you store, how you access it, the throughput, and how you partition and shard; you cannot use a database as a black box.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just cannot use something as a black box.

statement: Storing massive blob values of, say, 4 MB each would make relational databases 'cry their heart out', while DynamoDB would work better; performance varies with what you store and how you query.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: then relational databases would cry their heart out. But DynamoDB would work better.
